newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa arrivals around 880,000 T by Feb 23.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa arrivals around 880,000 T by Feb 23.

text.p: Cocoa arrivals at Ivorian ports were around 880,000 tonnes by February 23, against 920,000 logged up to February 24 in the record 1995/96 season, industry sources say.
"Arrivals are coming in at about half the rate seen earlier in the month (50,000 tonnes a week)," said one port source.
Figures compiled by February 23 suggested cumulative totals of 620,000 tonnes taken to Abidjan and 260,000 to the second Ivorian port of San Pedro since October 1.
Arrivals of cocoa at both ports by February 10 were around 820,000 tonnes but exporters said the weekly rate had slipped since mid-February to around 25,000 tonnes.
Upcountry buyers predict a small upswing in volumes of cocoa sent to ports from March after exporters completed a rush of coffee conditioning to meet late-February shipment deadlines.
Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonnes of cocoa in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) after a larger than expected 200,00 tonne midcrop (April-Sept). It forecasts 950,000 tonnes for 1996/97.

"There should be a bit more in March than we have seen in the past week or so," said one central Ivory Coast buyer operating around Gagnoa. "We should easily reach the (Ivorian 1996/97 year crop) forecast before the mid-crop (April-Sept) begins," the buyer added, referring to Ivory Coast's 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) crop forecast.
In 1995/96, arrivals totalled over 100,000 between late February and the end of the main crop in late March.
Average bean sizes this week remained at main crop (Oct-March) levels, between 95-100 beans per 100 grammes with humidity around eight percent, quality inspectors said.
Both figures are within the respective export standards of 105 beans per 100 grammes and eight percent humidity. One exporter said there had been some quality problems with slaty and mouldy beans.
"Officially, there is no midcrop this year." said one exporters. "If small beans are received we are supposed to refuse them," he added.
Some exporters have noted lax farming techniques in some areas. "Some farmers did not allow the beans to ferment for long enough, about 7-8 days," said one Abidjan-based exporter.

Others point to crush damage to cocoa stacked for weeks in Ivorian warehouses. Warehouses have been full to capacity around 400,000 tonnes for several weeks after exporters failed to ship cocoa against December contracts amid low world prices and demand.
Some exporters have been holding out for better prices in March.
European industry representatives recently in Ivory Coast called for tighter quality checks to ensure main and midcrop cocoa with differing bean sizes and quality were not mixed together.

Attention is still focused on weather to determine arrivals prospects up to October. Upcountry buyers and crop researchers say hot, dry weather over the past month had not yet damaged trees beyond stress tolerance levels, but arrivals from March could be affected if rains did not become heavier by early March.
"We are now seeing some rain in places. If the pattern develops into early March the trees should be okay," said one upcountry buyer based in Daloa.
Insufficient rain would raise flower and early pod mortality rates and reduce bean sizes in older pods.

Arrivals of cocoa at Ivorian ports to date suggest a total 1996/97 crop of well over one million tonnes, depending on the eventual shape of this year's so-far promising mid-crop, local crop analysts have said. --Abidjan newsroom + 225 21 90 90
